title: The orphan tsunami
teaches: How buried marshes, dead cedars, Japanese records and Indigenous stories showed that Cascadia's megathrust broke in a magnitude 9 earthquake on 26 January 1700

blocks.text: Around midnight between 27 and 28 January 1700 by the Western calendar, a tsunami came ashore along about 1,000 kilometres of the Pacific coast of Japan, from northern Honshu to the Kii Peninsula. At Miyako the sea flooded houses and fields, and the flooding set off a fire that burned houses; at Tanabe the flood ran into rice paddies and storehouses. Officials and merchants wrote it down, as they recorded everything that affected taxes and rice. What puzzled them was that nobody had felt an earthquake. In Japan tsunamis follow earthquakes, and this one had come out of a calm night. It was a tsunami without a parent: an orphan.

For nearly three centuries no one connected those records with anything. On the other side of the Pacific, the Cascadia subduction zone, where the Juan de Fuca plate sinks beneath the coast from northern California to Vancouver Island (lesson 11), had produced no large earthquake in the two hundred years of written history in the Pacific Northwest. Some geologists suspected it slid smoothly, without locking at all.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Around midnight between 27 and 28 January 1700 (Japanese time), a tsunami flooded about 1,000 km of the Japanese coast with no earthquake felt there.
Cascadia had no large earthquake in written history, and some geologists thought it might not lock.

blocks.text: In 1986 Brian Atwater of the US Geological Survey paddled a canoe up the tidal rivers of southwest Washington, looking at the banks at low tide. In the mud of the riverbanks around Willapa Bay he found the tops of old marshes: dark soils full of the roots of marsh plants, and in places the stumps of spruce trees, buried under grey tidal mud. Lesson 20 showed what that means. A marsh grows only around the level of high tide. To be buried under tidal mud, the ground beneath it must have dropped suddenly, a metre or two, into the reach of the tides. The soils were often capped by a thin layer of sand that thinned inland, the kind a tsunami leaves.

blocks.caption: A cut through a tidal marsh at the edge of a bay on the Washington coast, over 3,500 years. Earthquakes drop the marsh into the reach of the tides; it is buried, then rebuilt.
blocks.task: Play the years until at least three soils are buried

blocks.text: Atwater found the same sequence in estuary after estuary along the Washington coast: buried soils stacked one above another, each recording a sudden drop. Along the Copalis River and other tidal rivers, the drop had left something more: **ghost forests**, stands of dead western red cedar still upright in the tidal marshes, killed when salt water flooded their roots. High-precision radiocarbon dates on drowned trees and plants said the land had dropped sometime between about 1680 and 1720. Radiocarbon could not do better than that, but tree rings could.

Red cedar rots very slowly, and its tree rings record each year it grew. David Yamaguchi, a tree-ring scientist, matched the rings of the dead cedars against those of living old trees nearby, ring by ring, to find the year of each dead tree's outermost ring. In 1997, with Atwater and others, he reported the result: in the roots of the dead trees, the last ring had grown in 1699, and the roots died before the growing season of 1700 began. The earthquake had struck in the winter between.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Buried marsh soils capped by tsunami sand and tidal mud show that the Washington coast dropped suddenly, again and again.
Ghost forests of red cedar were killed by salt water when the land dropped.
Tree rings dated the death of the cedars to the winter of 1699–1700.

blocks.text: A winter of 1699–1700 at Cascadia pointed straight at the orphan tsunami. In 1996 Kenji Satake and colleagues worked through the old Japanese records of the wave, how high it rose and when it arrived at each place, and computed backwards. A tsunami crosses the deep ocean at the speed of a long wave. Its wavelength is hundreds of kilometres, far longer than the ocean is deep, so the whole water column moves with it and its speed is set only by the depth of the water: about 700 to 800 kilometres an hour over the deep Pacific. From the Cascadia coast to Japan takes about ten hours. Working back from the arrival times, the earthquake had struck at about nine o'clock at night, Pacific time, on 26 January 1700. Japan's clock runs 17 hours ahead of the Pacific coast's, so that was about two in the afternoon of 27 January in Japan, and ten hours later the wave arrived around midnight.

blocks.caption: The North Pacific, with a tsunami spreading from the Cascadia margin. The travel times come from the depth of the ocean.
blocks.task: Play the hours until the wave reaches Japan

blocks.text: The height of the wave in Japan told them the size. To raise a wave several metres high on the far side of the Pacific, the earthquake must have broken the whole length of the subduction zone, about 1,000 kilometres, in one magnitude 9 earthquake, much like Alaska in 1964.

People on the coast had their own record. Peoples of the coast from Vancouver Island to northern California tell of a night when the ground shook and the sea came in and swept villages away. The Huu-ay-aht First Nation's account tells how the people of Pachena Bay on Vancouver Island were lost in a flood one winter night. In 2005 the seismologist Ruth Ludwin and colleagues gathered such accounts, and many fit a winter night about three hundred years ago.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Satake's team worked back from the times and heights of the tsunami in Japan to an earthquake at about 9 p.m. on 26 January 1700.
Only a magnitude 9 earthquake rupturing the whole Cascadia subduction zone could make that wave.
Indigenous oral histories along the coast describe the same event.

blocks.text: The buried soils go back further than 1700. Atwater's marshes, which span 3,500 years, and layers of muddy sand that undersea landslides shook loose into the deep sea, record about twenty great Cascadia earthquakes over the past 10,000 years, at intervals from a couple of centuries to a thousand years, about 500 years on average. The plates are locked again today. GPS stations on the coast show it is being squeezed and dragged down exactly as lesson 20's figure shows between earthquakes.

Building codes in Washington, Oregon and British Columbia were updated from the 1990s onwards to plan for a magnitude 9 earthquake, and coastal towns now have tsunami evacuation routes and towers. For the people there, the important part is the warning that the earthquake itself gives: on the coast, strong shaking that lasts for minutes means go to high ground at once, because the tsunami may arrive in 15 to 30 minutes.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Buried soils and deep-sea deposits record about twenty great Cascadia earthquakes over 10,000 years, on average about 500 years apart.
The megathrust is locked again today, and the region now plans for a magnitude 9 earthquake and tsunami.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the orphan tsunami
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why did the 1700 tsunami puzzle the people who recorded it in Japan?
choices: Nobody in Japan had felt an earthquake before it
It came in the middle of summer
items.why: Tsunamis in Japan normally follow local earthquakes. This one arrived from an earthquake on the far side of the Pacific.

items.ask: What does a marsh soil buried under tidal mud tell a geologist?
choices: The ground beneath it dropped suddenly into the reach of the tides
The sea slowly rose over thousands of years
items.why: Marshes grow only near high tide; a sharp contact from soil to tidal mud means a sudden drop.

items.ask: How did Yamaguchi date the earthquake to the winter of 1699–1700?
choices: He matched the rings of dead cedars against living trees and found their last ring grew in 1699
He used radiocarbon on the cedars
He counted the layers of mud above the trees
items.why: Tree rings give calendar years. The dead cedars stopped growing after the 1699 season and before 1700's.

items.ask: How did Satake's team find the hour of the earthquake?
choices: They worked back from the tsunami's arrival times in Japan, using the speed of a wave across the deep Pacific
items.why: A tsunami's speed depends on the ocean depth, about 10 hours from Cascadia to Japan, so arrival times give the time of the earthquake.

items.ask: Why must the 1700 earthquake have been about magnitude 9?
choices: Only a rupture along the whole 1,000 km subduction zone could make a wave that high in Japan
Because it was felt in Japan
items.why: A smaller earthquake breaking part of the fault would have made a much smaller wave on the far side of the ocean.

items.ask: You are on the Washington coast and the ground shakes hard for over a minute. What should you do?
choices: Go to high ground at once, without waiting for an official warning
Go to the beach to watch the sea
items.why: A Cascadia tsunami can arrive within 15 to 30 minutes; the shaking itself is the warning.

summary: **Japan recorded an orphan tsunami.** In January 1700 a wave hit 1,000 km of coast with no earthquake felt.
**Cascadia's coast dropped suddenly.** Atwater found marsh soils buried under tsunami sand and tidal mud.
**Ghost forests date it to the winter of 1699–1700.** Yamaguchi's tree rings showed the cedars' last ring was 1699.
**The wave took about ten hours to cross.** Satake worked back to about 9 p.m. on 26 January 1700.
**It was a magnitude 9.** Only the whole subduction zone breaking could make that wave.
**Oral histories record it too.** Coastal peoples tell of a winter night of shaking and flooding.
**It will happen again.** About twenty great earthquakes have struck in 10,000 years, and the fault is locked now.
